pairs.rationale: Both describe gifts or sacrifices unable to perfect the worshiper. The earlier unit explicitly concerns conscience; here the law is a shadow and repeated yearly sacrifices cannot perfect those approaching. The particular images and stated effects remain distinct.

The earlier statement that gifts and sacrifices cannot perfect conscience explains the subject beside this rhetorical question about offerings ceasing after definitive cleansing. The question is not rewritten as an assertion that the offerings actually ceased.

The annual atonement statute provides a concrete year-by-year sacrificial setting beside the reminder of sins year by year. The statute and Hebrews' assessment of repeated reminders retain their different statements.

pairs.relationship: animal blood and its stated limits
pairs.rationale: Both name animal blood in discussing purification. The earlier unit describes flesh-related cleansing, while this unit denies taking sins away by bulls and goats. The different objects and effects are kept rather than presenting them as identical claims.

pairs.relationship: quotation with body and ears difference
pairs.rationale: The sacrifice-and-offering rejection corresponds to Psalm39:7. Hebrews then says a body was prepared; the supplied Psalm says ears were prepared and also mentions burnt and sin offerings. The actual body/ears difference is preserved.

The burnt-offering and sin-offering saying corresponds to the latter part of Psalm39:7. Hebrews speaks of taking no pleasure, while the Psalm says not requested. The verbs and the Psalm's additional ears clause remain distinct.

The scroll-of-the-book, coming and doing-God's-will clauses correspond to these two Psalm units. The Psalm says I desired to do Thy will and adds law within the belly; Hebrews presents coming to do the will. The wording and boundaries remain as printed.

This summarizes the earlier sacrifice, offering, burnt-offering and sin-offering saying found in Psalm39:7. Hebrews adds its offered-according-to-law explanation; that explanation is not inserted into the Psalm unit.

pairs.relationship: first and second statements in context
pairs.rationale: The earlier quoted statements provide the sequence behind He then said and the first/second contrast. Sacrificial non-desire precedes coming to do God's will. The reference does not substitute an unprinted universal definition for first and second.

Both describe a decisive self-related offering rather than an endless sequence. The earlier unit says He offered Himself once for all; this names the body of Jesus Christ and sanctification by that will. The added predicates remain in their own units.

Daily standing and repeated priestly offerings are compared with the same chapter's yearly sacrifices unable to perfect. Daily/yearly, standing and shadow language remain distinct descriptions within the shared repetition argument.

The seated-at-the-right-hand statement corresponds to the Psalm command to sit at the right hand. Hebrews adds the one sacrifice for sins for all time; the Psalm has the Lord speak to my lord and mentions enemies as footstool. Its wording does not print the whole sacrifice claim.

The waiting-until-enemies-become-footstool clause directly corresponds to the Psalm right-hand saying. The source continues the preceding seated-sacrificer account; the Psalm does not itself give that whole sacrificial context.

Both connect the one offering with sanctification. The earlier unit says we have been sanctified through Jesus' body once for all; here one offering perfects for all time those being sanctified. The actual verbal forms are not collapsed.

The following covenant-law and non-remembrance sayings supply the testimony introduced here. The introduction attributes testimony to the Holy Spirit; the following units preserve their own Lord-says and He-adds wording without naming an unprinted human author.

The covenant-law promise corresponds to native Greek-based Jeremiah38:33. Hebrews puts laws upon hearts and inscription upon mind; Jeremiah says laws into understanding and writing upon hearts, and names Israel's house. The placement, nouns and recipients remain distinct.

The promise not to remember sins corresponds to the end of Jeremiah38:34. Hebrews also names lawless deeds; Jeremiah supplies its own surrounding knowledge and mercy clauses. Neither selected unit is completed with unprinted clauses from the other.

The foregoing non-remembrance promise is the immediate premise for the conclusion about forgiveness and no further sin offering. The pair follows the internal argument without turning the target promise into the exact words of the resulting inference.

The earlier account of entry by His own blood gives a concrete counterpart for the readers' confidence of entry in Jesus' blood. The subjects and the earlier once/eternal-redemption description remain distinct.

Matthew narrates the sanctuary veil torn in two; Hebrews calls the entry curtain His flesh. The actual veil/curtain wording is retained, and Matthew's narrative does not itself print that flesh explanation or the whole new-and-living-way claim.

The earlier exhortation explicitly names Jesus as apostle and high priest of the confession. That priest title supplies a concrete comparison for the great priest here in the Jesus-blood context. The house-of-God clause and apostle title remain distinct.

The water-cleansing and renewed-heart promise supplies specific cleansing and heart images beside the sprinkled hearts and water-washed body. Ezekiel's promise and Hebrews approach exhortation retain their different objects; no exclusive rite is inferred.

Sarah's considering the One who promised faithful gives a concrete same-letter counterpart to the Promiser's faithfulness supporting steadfast hope. Sarah's conception circumstances are not transferred to the readers confession instruction.

Both connect love with action toward one another. Galatians says to serve one another through love; Hebrews calls for mutual consideration that stirs love and good works. Their exhortations and surrounding freedom discussion remain distinct.

Both call for mutual encouragement with a stated time emphasis. The earlier unit specifies each day during Today to resist hardening; this names gathering and the approaching day. Today and the approaching day are not treated as identical dates.

Numbers contrasts unintentional sin with a goat offering and an act with a presumptuous hand that treats God's word as worthless and brings destruction from the people. Hebrews warns of deliberate sin after truth with no sacrifice remaining. The settings and stated consequences remain distinct.

Isaiah says fire will consume the opponents; Hebrews names a fury of fire about to consume the adversaries and fearful judgment. The fire-and-opponent correspondence is specific, while the prophetic circumstances and all surrounding claims are not made identical.

pairs.relationship: two or three witnesses in death sentence
pairs.rationale: Deuteronomy explicitly requires two or three witnesses for a death sentence rather than one. Hebrews recalls the Mosaic threshold in its warning argument. The original case setting and the later application are not collapsed.

Both warn about rejection after described religious benefits and name the Son. Chapter6 describes enlightenment, shared Spirit and falling away; here the warning names covenant blood, trampling and insulting the Spirit of grace. No unstated identity or final theory is imposed on the sanctified pronoun.

The vengeance-and-repayment saying corresponds to native Deuteronomy32:35. The exact first-person and timing formulations are retained rather than importing every word of one quotation into the other supplied unit.

The Lord-judging-His-people saying corresponds to Deuteronomy32:36. The target also contains its own account of His servants and their condition; Hebrews uses the saying within the preceding warning. This second pair adds no second source completion.

pairs.relationship: falling into the Lord's hands contrast
pairs.rationale: David chooses falling into the Lord's hand because His compassions are very many; Hebrews stresses the fearfulness of falling into the living God's hands. The related phrase preserves singular/plural hand wording, the distinct circumstances and the stated contrast in attitude.

Both refer to enlightenment as a prior religious benefit. Chapter6 names it among other experiences; here readers recall their earlier enlightened days and endurance of suffering. The reference does not identify every person or consequence as the same.

Corinthians describes apostles as a spectacle to the world, angels and human beings; Hebrews recalls public exposure to reproach and affliction. The different groups and the additional companionship clause are not made identical events.

The later instruction to remember prisoners as fellow prisoners supplies a concrete counterpart to sympathy with prisoners here. The actual prisoners wording is retained; no my-bonds variant or author identity is inserted.

The earlier confidence for entry in Jesus' blood supplies a concrete basis beside the warning not to discard confidence. This verse adds great reward; the entry description and reward statement remain distinct.

Both connect persevering trust with receiving promised benefit. Chapter6 names faith and patience inheriting promises; this unit names endurance and doing God's will to receive the promise. The verbs and scope retain their own forms.

The coming-without-delay saying corresponds to Habakkuk2:3. The prophetic unit speaks in its vision setting; Hebrews says the coming One and a very little while. The wording does not by itself identify every referent or calculate a date.

Hebrews says My righteous one will live by faith; Habakkuk says the righteous one shall live by My faithfulness. The drawing-back/displeasure clause comes before the faith clause in Habakkuk and after it here. Possessives, faith/faithfulness and clause order remain distinct.

pairs.relationship: response to faith and drawing back contrast
pairs.rationale: The preceding faith/drawing-back quotation supplies the alternatives beside the writer's we assertion. This unit names destruction and preservation of the soul; those consequences are not silently inserted into the preceding quotation.

Both speak of faith apart from ordinary sight. Corinthians describes walking through faith rather than sight; Hebrews describes assurance of hoped-for things and conviction concerning unseen realities. Their precise definitions and surrounding situations remain distinct.

The following Abel account is an explicit example of testimony through faith: he receives testimony of righteousness. This provides a concrete instance of the elders' testimony rather than reducing every elder to Abel or supplying all later examples in one verse.

Genesis narrates God making heaven and earth and speaking light into being. Hebrews names the ages formed by God's word and adds an inference about visible things. Genesis does not itself print that entire unseen-origin formulation.

Genesis narrates Cain and Abel bringing gifts and the Lord's differing regard for them. Hebrews gives its faith-and-righteousness interpretation and the dead-still-speaking statement. Those explanatory clauses are not silently inserted into the Genesis narrative.

The Enoch account corresponds to pleasing God and no longer being found because God took him. The actual supplied removal wording and Hebrews' added faith/no-death interpretation remain as printed rather than substituting a familiar other-edition formulation.

pairs.relationship: pleasing God through faith in context
pairs.rationale: The preceding Enoch account explicitly connects faith and testimony that he pleased God. It provides the immediate case beside this faith requirement. This verse additionally names believing God is and rewards seekers, which are not all repeated in the Enoch unit.

Genesis gives the announced flood, ark entry for Noah's household and his compliance with God's commands. Hebrews describes faith, unseen warning and the resulting righteousness account. The latter interpretive predicates are not substituted for the narrative instructions.

pairs.relationship: call to leave for a shown land
pairs.rationale: Genesis commands Abram to leave for the land God will show and narrates his departure. Hebrews names Abraham and describes obedience through faith without knowing the destination. The printed Abram/Abraham forms and the additional promises remain distinct.

Genesis names Jacob coming to Isaac where Abraham and Isaac lived as strangers. This gives a concrete place-and-patriarch counterpart to the sojourning description. Its unit does not say all three lived in tents together at one time.

The later explanation says God prepared a city for those desiring a heavenly homeland. This gives an explicit divine-city counterpart to awaiting the city whose maker is God. Neither unit is completed with an unprinted city name.

Genesis narrates the Lord doing for Sarah as He spoke and her bearing the promised son. This provides the narrative promise counterpart to her considering the Promiser faithful. Hebrews adds its faith, barrenness and beyond-age descriptions.

The promise that offspring will multiply like heavens stars and seashore sand corresponds to the two images here. Genesis gives the promise; Hebrews describes the multitude born from one as good as dead. The promise and fulfillment descriptions remain distinct.

Abraham calls himself a resident foreigner and a sojourner while requesting burial land. This gives a concrete confession beside Hebrews' strangers-and-sojourners wording. Abraham is alive in that Genesis scene; the source's account of dying in faith is not inserted into it.

The preceding confession of being strangers and sojourners supplies the stated words behind those who say such things. Hebrews then infers seeking a homeland. The inference is distinguished from the quoted confession itself.

pairs.relationship: return to the departure country discussed
pairs.rationale: Genesis discusses taking Abraham's son back to the country of departure and records Abraham's refusal. This is a specific return-country comparison for Hebrews counterfactual opportunity statement, without claiming every patriarch made that exact narrated decision.

pairs.relationship: God called God of the patriarchs
pairs.rationale: God's self-identification as God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob supplies a concrete counterpart to being called their God. Hebrews adds not being ashamed, a better heavenly homeland and a prepared city; those clauses are not inserted into Exodus.

Genesis narrates the test, commanded offering, binding and halted killing of Isaac, calling him beloved. Hebrews describes offering by faith and calls him only son. The son descriptors and distinction between offering and completed killing remain as printed.

The in-Isaac offspring declaration directly corresponds to Genesis21:12. The Genesis unit also addresses Sarah's words and the other child context; Hebrews quotes the declaration within the Isaac-offering account without reproducing every surrounding clause.

pairs.relationship: Abraham faith and God giving life to dead
pairs.rationale: Both associate Abraham-related faith with God's power over death. Romans names God giving life to the dead; Hebrews reasons that He can raise the dead and calls Isaac's reception figurative. No literal completed death of Isaac is asserted.

This part of Genesis gives the blessing spoken to Jacob, one of the two sons named here. Hebrews additionally names Esau and faith concerning things to come. This pair covers Jacob's portion rather than claiming the target also narrates Esau's blessing.

This separate part of Genesis gives Isaac's words to Esau. Together with the separately retained Jacob passage it supplies both named blessings, while the distinct words and circumstances remain intact. The second pair adds no second source completion.

The Genesis worship-and-staff statement gives a concrete counterpart for this part of the Jacob account. The selected unit does not itself narrate both grandsons' blessings; the separate blessing passage supplies that part.

Genesis narrates the hands placed over Joseph's two sons and the blessing requesting blessing for the children. It supplies the blessing context beside the staff-worship comparison retained separately. Neither pair adds a second completion for this source.

Genesis records Joseph nearing death, promising God's visitation and departure, and requiring his bones carried up. Those concrete clauses correspond to the exodus-and-bones summary; Hebrews adds by-faith interpretation.

Exodus gives the male-child decree and a beautiful child hidden for three months, using they hid after she conceived. Hebrews explicitly names his parents and lack of fear. The pronouns and added fear statement remain distinct.

pairs.relationship: royal adoption and grown Moses brothers
pairs.rationale: Exodus narrates becoming Pharaoh's daughter's son and grown Moses going to his brothers and seeing their suffering. Hebrews explicitly calls this a refusal by faith. No formal renunciation scene or particular unprinted motive is added to the Exodus units.

The preceding refusal of Pharaoh's daughter's son status supplies the action explained by this choosing-rather clause. Here the people-of-God mistreatment and temporary pleasure of sin give the contrast; those motives are not all printed in the preceding single unit.

The later exhortation to bear His reproach outside the camp supplies a concrete reproach counterpart to Christ-related reproach valued above Egypt's treasures. The addressees action and Moses' valuation are not treated as the same historical event.

pairs.relationship: not fearing the king in different cases
pairs.rationale: Both accounts explicitly deny fear of the king: the parents do not fear the decree, and Moses does not fear the king’s anger at departure. Their actors, actions and the seeing-the-invisible description remain distinct. No unprinted identification of this departure with another fear narrative is required.

The Passover instructions name slaughter, blood on door parts and protection from the destroyer entering the houses. These provide concrete counterparts to Passover, sprinkled blood and the firstborn warning. The particular verbs and full instructions remain as printed.

pairs.relationship: Egyptian waters and Israel dry crossing
pairs.rationale: Exodus contrasts the returning waters over Egypt's forces with Israel walking on dry ground amid the sea. Hebrews describes the crossing through faith and Egyptians being swallowed when attempting it. The narrative and interpretive summary retain their different forms.

pairs.relationship: Jericho days circuits and falling wall
pairs.rationale: Joshua records six days, six circuits on the seventh day in6:15, the seventh circuit in6:16 and the wall falling in6:20. Hebrews summarizes encirclement for seven days. The day/circuit distinction and the supplied six/seventh verse division are preserved.

Joshua narrates Rahab, called the harlot, and her household being brought out because she hid the spies. Hebrews says prostitute and adds faith, receiving spies in peace and disobedient others. Their actual descriptors, actions and added faith interpretation remain distinct.

Acts names judges until Samuel the prophet, providing a specific counterpart for Samuel in this abbreviated list. It is not represented as naming every other listed person or supplying every exploit of the prophets.

Daniel reports righteousness found in him and God saving him from lions, which had not troubled him. This is a concrete lion-rescue counterpart to the righteousness and lion-mouth clauses. This supplied passage does not explicitly name an angel or closed mouths, and no whole anonymous group is identified.

pairs.relationship: fire unable to harm the faithful
pairs.rationale: Daniel names the angel with Azariah and companions, flame shaken out and fire not touching or troubling them. This gives a concrete fire-power counterpart. Hebrews does not name those actors or state that every sword, weakness and battle clause describes the same people.

pairs.relationship: child restored and returned to mother
pairs.rationale: The narrative of the child living and being given back to his mother supplies a specific instance beside women receiving their dead through resurrection. The other half of Hebrews unit concerns different tortured people and is compared separately.

The brother refuses during torture and expects the King of the world to raise those dying for His laws to everlasting renewal. This supplies specific torture-and-resurrection-hope correspondence. His release-from-present-life phrase describes death; it is not equated with Hebrews unaccepted release.

Acts narrates Paul and Silas being beaten and confined in prison with secured feet. These give concrete counterparts to flogging and imprisonment in the list. The target is not represented as explicitly naming every mockery or chain clause, or as identifying every anonymous sufferer.

The Spirit-clothed priest Azarias is stoned by King Joash's command in the courtyard of the Lord's house. This provides a concrete stoning counterpart. The reference does not identify an unnamed sawn-apart person or make its victim every person or death in the list.

Elijah's cave scene and report of slain prophets and pursuit of his life supply a specific cave-and-persecution comparison. Hebrews gives a wider wandering list and the world-not-worthy judgment, which are not all printed in this narrative.

Both summarize the listed people as faithful while not receiving what was promised. Verse13 says promises and recalls dying and distant greeting; this says the promise and testimony through faith. The singular/plural and surrounding assertions remain without an added theory about every other promise.

The earlier law-perfected-nothing and better-hope statement supplies a concrete better/perfection comparison. Here God provides something better concerning us and perfection not apart from us. The scope, participants and exact statements retain their own wording.
